steps.title: A poem in one breath
paragraphs:
An old silent pond.
A frog jumps into the pond.
Splash! Silence again.
This poem was written in Japan over 300 years ago by a poet called Bashō. It's only seventeen syllables long, yet you can see the pond, hear the splash, and feel the quiet afterwards.
That's a haiku: a whole moment in one breath.

cards.title: Haiku
cards.body: A haiku is a three-line poem from Japan. The lines have 5, 7 and 5 syllables. It catches one small moment, often from nature, so clearly that the reader can see it. Many haiku hide a season word, and end with a small surprise.

cards.title: Counting syllables
cards.body: A syllable is a beat in a word. Clap as you say it: “frog” (1), “ri-ver” (2), “but-ter-fly” (3). The counter in your workspace counts for you, but it can make mistakes, so clap to check and tap a word to fix its count.

cards.title: Tell it, or picture it?
cards.telling:
Autumn is beautiful
and makes me feel peaceful
I love the season
cards.showing:
Red leaves on the path
crunch beneath my muddy boots.
One leaf still falling.
cards.note: The second haiku never says “beautiful” or “peaceful”. It shows a picture, and the feeling comes by itself.

cards.title: The surprise
cards.prompt: Tap the two words in the last line that surprise you.
cards.text:
Morning cereal
spoon halfway towards my mouth.
The cat drinks my milk.

prompts: Which of your three haiku shows its moment most clearly? Why?
Did you have to change a word to make a line fit? What did you choose instead?
